newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - BMW, Chrysler in Latam motor tieup.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - BMW, Chrysler in Latam motor tieup.

text.p: Car making giants Bayerischen Motoren Werke (BMW) and Chrysler Corp announced on Tuesday they would invest up to $500 million to establish a South American joint venture to produce small car engines.

BMW Chairman Bernd Pischetsrieder and Chrysler Chairman Robert Eaton told reporters at the Paris car show that the 50/50 project should produce up to 400,000 four-cylinder car engines a year and should start operation by the end of 1999.

The car makers said a specific location has not yet been found, but that engines produced by the joint venture will be used in cars from BMWs Rover Group unit and the Chrysler Neon which is made in the U.S.
The deal was aimed at achieving economies of scale in engine production that could not be achieved alone.

"Developing new engine families is a costly business, and partnering in this way makes good economic and business sense, Eaton said. "We have looked at making small engines, but it did not make sense at 200,000. 400,000 is considered the optimum capacity."
The move comes as a bold step for both companies which are hoping to win a larger share of what is expected to become a fast growing market for small-sized cars over the next 10-years.
The 1.4 and 1.6 liter engines will be based on a Chrysler design.
Part of the reason for opening a plant in South America was to develop a stronger foothold in what is expected to be a fast growing market there.

"Looking back at the last five years, we see an increase in the region by more than 100 per cent, making Latin America currently the fastest growing area worldwide for the automobile industry," BMWs Pischetsrieder said.

The move was BMWs first foray into Latin America, but the second such announcement for Chrysler in the last 45 days. In August, the U.S. car maker announced plans to build a plant in Brazil to produce pickup trucks for distribution in Latin America.

Pischetsrieder said the decision to produce engines in South America did not disrupt its hopes of founding another engine facility in the Britain which would make larger engines than those made with Chrysler.
He added that the new engine will replace Rovers A series which was originally designed in the 1950s.
The BMW Chairman said he was now in talks with the British government for subsidies for the plant and that the deal would go forward if government help is granted.
Chrysler Chairman Eaton was quick to play down speculation that the new plant would cost U.S. jobs, saying it "increases the saleability of small" cars in the U.S., thus creating jobs.

The joint-venture should help dispell doubts that BMW was loosing faith in its Rover unit, which after being bought in 1994 from Japan's Honda has steadily lost money and required huge cash infusions from BMW.
